A genus of c. 110 species, mostly in Malesia, but distributed from Madagascar and the Seychelles to Sri Lanka, NE India, Thailand, Indo-China, throughout Malesia to Australia and the Solomon Is. and New Caledonia
Most species are found in Borneo (31) and Sumatra (29), with 10 species recorded from Peninsular Malaysia
Most lowland species in Peninsular Malaysia are widespread from Indo-China to Australia with the exception of Nepenthes benstonei that is endemic to NE Peninsular Malaysia
In contrast, the montane species are all endemic: N. sanguinea is the most widespread (with one record from Thailand), in contrast N. gracillima and N. ramispina have more restricted distributions.
Nepenthes species are often locally common
In general they are intolerant of deep shade

Lowland species occur from sea-level to c. 700(--1000) m altitude and are most frequently encountered on moist, nutrient-poor soil in heath forest or open secondary forest or in thickets of the resam fern (Dicranopteris linearis (N.T.Burm.) Underw.) or for N. ampullaria and N. mirabilis in swampy areas
Often more than not one species occurs in the same locality but the common species are slightly different in their ecological preferences (Green, Gard

The montane Nepenthes species are confined to upper montane forest between 1500--2000 m altitude, usually on peat soil in open mossy, stunted, ridge-top forest where N. sanguinea is sometimes also found as an epiphyte
Unlike in Borneo, no species is found on limestone.
J. 1 (1940) 35) reported that Nepenthes species flower seasonally but Chua (J. Trop
Sci. 12 (2000) 377) observed flowering peaks when most plants flower gregariously, but inflorescences are produced sporadically throughout the year
Being dioecious, all Nepenthes species are obligate outbreeders
Chua (2000) demonstrated that in N. macfarlanei without pollination (bagged flowers) no seed was set compared with open pollinated flowers where 60% set fruit
In N. gracilis, Green (1967) observed that most flowers set fruit

Nepenthes flowers are adapted for generalist entomophilous pollination –flowers are held exposed on erect inflorescences above neighbouring vegetation, sessile glands cover the entire adaxial tepal surface with nectar and the anther heads release pollen in sticky tetrads
However, for most species the effective pollinator is not known
That large numbers of seeds are produced is probably due to the long period of pollen viability–three days in N. gracilis (Lim & Prakash, Malay
J. Sci. 2 (1973) 45) and exceptionally long stigma receptivity–23 days in N. macfarlanei (Chua, 2000)
In N. gracilis pollen is shed between 1600 and 1800 h when both the male and female flowers emit a heavy foetid smell (Lim & Prakash, 1973)
Malay., 2001) reported that this species is pollinated by moths
For N. macfarlanei, Chua (2000) observed flower odour as slightly musky or foetid, stigmas were receptive throughout the day while pollen was released between 0600--1400(--1700) h
She suggested muscid flies as the pollinators because they occasionally visited the flowers
Clarke (2001) recorded that N. ampullaria flowers produce a ‘foul musky smell’ in daytime and suggested pollination by carrion flies
Malesiana 1, 15 (2001) 4) noted that inflorescences of N. mirabilis smelled of mice droppings but its pollinator remains unknown
For example, an inflorescence of N. macfarlanei can produce about 2,800 seeds based on an average of 60 mature seeds per fruit and 46 fruits per inflorescence (Chua, 2000)

Lim & Prakash (1973) counted between 50 and 200 fruits per inflorescence in N. gracilis, with large fruits averaging 145 seeds and smaller ones about 23 seeds, while Green (1967) reported that a single inflorescence of this species could produce 10,000 seeds
At maturity, the capsule valves open slightly allowing the light seeds with air-filled, thread-like appendages to be blown away by gusts of wind
If sown straight from the fruit, seed viability of N. gracilis is c. 80% but drops to c. 17% after 4 days (Lim & Prakash, 1973)
Most seeds germinate within 2--3 weeks with a small proportion remaining viable for 6--7 months (Green, 1967)

J. 32 (1978) 105) obtained similar results for N. rafflesiana and observed that the first leaf with a minature pitcher was produced after 20--30 days after which seedling leaves were produced roughly every 30 days, the fourth being the first pitcher to trap ants
Young plants of N. gracilis grow very slowly and remain as a tiny rosette of leaves for 2--3 years (Green, 1967).

Peninsular Malaysian Nepenthes species begin life as a low rosette with an extremely short, erect stem and short internodes, then become shrubby by the production of short stems 1--2 m tall with longer internodes, and finally become lianas with climbing stems and even longer internodes, the stems being supported by the twining leaf tendrils
Nepenthes ampullaria may proceed from the rosette to the climbing stage with a neglible short-stem stage
This species is also unusual in sometimes producing short axillary rosette stems from the lower 1--2 m of its climbing stems
The leaves of Nepenthes species are highly specialised
The ‘leaf lamina’ bears at its tip a tendril from which arises a sharply upturned and hollow pitcher, with a more-or-less oblique mouth overhung by a lid, from the base of which arises a short spur
Venation suggests that this spur is the true leaf apex
The lid, being the only organ to lack a midrib, may be derived from a modified pair of leaflets
In all species the leaves of both short stems and climbing stems tend to be more markedly petiolate than those of the rosette stems
The waxy zone covers about one third of the inner wall in upper pitchers with its white ‘bloom’ of minute, wax scales, below is the glossy glandular zone
The lower pitchers have a larger waxy zone, except in N. ampullaria where it is very small
The shape, venation and indumentum of the lid are of taxonomic importance
In most species, the size, nature and distribution of the nectar glands on the lower surface of the lid are important characters.
During development, the mouth of the pitcher is hermetically sealed by the lid that only opens when the final size of the pitcher has been approached
Unopened pitchers contain several millilitres of fluid
Once open, the lid is usually held a little above the mouth, and probably serves to shelter the open mouth from rain
Nepenthes ampullaria is an exception with its narrow lid reflexed away from the mouth
In most species, the pitchers act as pitfall traps for a wide range of invertebrates and, less commonly, vertebrates.

Once open, the fluid in the pitchers begins to harbour a succession of microscopic organisms, such as bacteria, desmids and diatoms, and rotifers that are food for mosquito larvae and water mites that are in turn preyed upon by carnivorous mosquito larvae
Carrion-feeding species consume the drowned prey; and detritus feeders, like mite and beetle larvae, feed on the accumulating organic debris in the bottom of the pitcher

Alfred Wallace (The Malay Archipelago, 1869, p. 182) was driven by thirst on Gunung Ledang to drink this ‘animal soup’ from the pitcher of N. sanguinea and wrote that ‘...the water contained in the pitchers (about half a pint in each) was full of insects and otherwise uninviting
On tasting it, however, we found it very palatable, though rather warm, and we all quenched our thirst from these natural jugs’
Cheek & Jebb (2001) tested the fluid from unopened pitchers and considered it potable
The complex food web has been described in some detail for pitchers of N. albomarginata by Beaver (Malay
J. 33 (1979) 1), who recorded 55 insect species (including 33 mosquito species) and 3 spiders
Faunal composition depends on the Nepenthes species
Several new species of fly and mosquito have been discovered living in pitchers
Beaver considered that about 79% of the fauna are dependent on pitchers as their habitat and in some cases live nowhere else

They complete their life cycles within a short period because most pitchers are short-lived, for example N. mirabilis pitchers live for less than a month (Clarke, 2001) and those of N. macfarlanei and N. ramispina for between 2.5--7.5 months (Kiew, J. Wildlife & Nat
In addition, several aquatic species are able to live in the fluid, such as tadpoles of four frog and one toad species (Kiew, 1990) and crabs (Ng & Lim, Malay
As long as they are alive, they are not affected by the proteolytic enzymes in the pitcher fluid but should they die they will immediately be digested
Above the fluid, the spider Misumenops nepenthicola is a common inhabitant of N. albomarginata, N. gracilis and N. rafflesiana pitchers
By spreading its web across the mouth of the pitcher, it highjacks the pitcher prey, as well as trapping insects emerging from their larval stage
If disturbed it dives into the fluid and stays below the surface until danger has passed
Another spider species, Xenoplatyurus beaveri, occupies the same niche in N. ampullaria (Clarke, 2001).

Prey is probably attracted to the pitcher by a combination of its colour and the presence of nectar secreted by glands on the underside of the pitcher lid, the inner edge of the peristome, and on the outer surface of the pitcher
The dense coating of minute, readily detachable wax scales in the waxy zone stick to the suction pads (tarsi) of insects, temporarily destroying their ability to grip any surface
The prey then drops into the fluid in the lower half of the pitcher, which contains a wetting agent, making escape more difficult

Once drowned, the combination of proteolytic enzymes secreted by the glands in the lower part of the pitcher and by bacteria living in the pitcher fluid leads to the breakdown of prey protein followed by absorption of the digested products by these same glands (Juniper et al., The Carnivorous Plant, 1989)
Several enzymes have been isolated from the pitcher fluid, such as nepenthesin, all of which are more effective in acid conditions
The acidity of pitcher fluid in N. gracilis ranges between pH 4 and 5 (Wee, 1978)
In N. mirabilis 60% of nitrogen in plant tissue is derived from prey (Schulze et al., Oecologia 112 (1997) 464) and Moran & Moran (Internat
Sci. 159 (1998) 996) observed a reduction in growth rate when pitchers were prevented from catching prey
Ants appear to be the single most important prey species of Nepenthes

However, a wide range of other invertebrates (bees and wasps, crickets and cockroaches, bugs and beetles, flies, dragonflies, moths and centipedes) are also caught, including a few vertebrates such as frogs and lizards and, very occasionally, a rat has been reported to have drowned in the pitchers of Bornean N. rajah that has the largest pitchers of any species (Phillipps & Lamb, Pitcher Plants of Borneo, 1996)

Nepenthes albomarginata is exceptional in its prey specificity trapping almost exclusively termites (95% of prey capture), which were observed to feed on the hairs that form the white band below the peristome

The unusual pitchers of N. ampullaria that have an erect lid and are long-lived may, instead of capturing animals as their primary prey, serve as litter-trapping devices and depend on bacterial symbionts for leaf decomposition (Clarke, 2001).
Apparently all species that grow sympatrically are capable of hybridizing under natural conditions

Their remarkable chromosomal uniformity (n = 40 in all species studied) is consistent with the ease with which fertile interspecific hybrids are produced in the wild and in horticulture (Cheek & Jebb, 2001)
Physiological barriers to interspecific hybridization also seem weak
Indeed, some cultivars have multiple species parentage
For lowland species, hybrid plants are infrequent compared with the parent species
Three have been named: Nepenthes xhookeriana (N. ampullaria x N. rafflesiana), N. xtrichocarpa (N. ampullaria x N. gracilis) and Nepenthes xghazallyiana (N. gracilis x N. mirabilis)
Rare hybrid plants have also been recorded between N. gracilis and N. rafflesiana, between N. gracilis and N. ampullaria, and between N. benstonei and N. mirabilis
Hybridization is frequent between all the montane species that occur together, which can make identification difficult
Kiew et al. (Telopea 10 (2000) 225) demonstrated conclusively using molecular techniques the hybrid origin of some of these putative lowland hybrids

Of the species-specific bands of the parental species, N. xhookeriana inherited additively 16 bands from N. rafflesiana and 14 from N. ampullaria and half the samples had one additional unique band; while N. xtrichocarpa had 22 bands in common with N. gracilis and 14 in common with N. ampullaria and had no unique bands; while the third hybrid had 20 bands in common with N. gracilis and 14 in common with N. rafflesiana and had no unique bands.
There are two main threats to Nepenthes species: the horticultural trade and habitat destruction
The horticultural trade in Nepenthes is mostly international with the main markets in Western Europe, Japan and the United States of America

Trade in wild plants has greatly decreased with the avaibility of tissue-cultured plants and the listing of all species of the genus Nepenthes on the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora CITES Appendix II, and N. khasiana (India) and N. rajah (restricted to the Kinabalu National Park, Sabah) which appear on Appendix I. However, local collecting of plants from the wild continues and Nepenthes species are now uncommon at Fraser’s Hill, Pahang, as is the white form of N. sanguinea at Cameron Highlands, Pahang
In Peninsular Malaysia, only N. benstonei is assessed as Endangered
However, given the threats above, it is likely that other Peninsular Malaysian endemic highland Nepenthes species also merit threatened status
The devastating effect of habitat disturbance is illustrated by the extinction of N. mirabilis from Singapore due to the elimination of its peat swamp forest habitat there.
The main value of Nepenthes is in the international horticultural trade
Cheek & Jebb (2001) reported it probably far exceeded 15 million US dollars per annum

Locally, stems of several species have been used for making rope: stems of N. ampullaria are said to be of particularly good quality being very durable, and in Penang ropes of N. mirabilis were used to drag fishing nets (FRI 9822)
Pitchers are used to cook rice, imparting an interesting flavour
Several species are reported to have minor medicinal use and one, N. rafflesiana, is used as a musical instrument.
It is important to be aware of the dimorphy of the pitchers when collecting Nepenthes
Collections of both upper and lower pitchers are important
Furthermore, as in the case of any dioecious taxon, separate collections of male and female plants from the same locality are desirable
Several species may grow together at the same locality
It is important not to overlook this possiblity, to look out for and collect potential second species, and to avoid making mixed collections

Particular care should be taken when pressing and mounting the pitcher so that the wings on the ventral surface, the peristome and, most important of all, the underside of the lid, are clearly visible
When mounting Nepenthes collections the surface (especially the inner surface) of the lid and the mouth must not be obscured, as this will make identification difficult.

Being dioecious, all Nepenthes species are obligate outbreeders
